extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalism students, editors and researchers interested in journalism ethics and media scandals
extracted.subtask_description: A case-study style biographical article documenting Stephen Glass's journalistic fabrications, editorial failures, and later legal and professional consequences; useful for examining standards of accuracy, sourcing, fact-checking, corrections, and moral fitness in journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy / truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories must be factually accurate; Glass's majority of stories were determined to be 'partially or entirely fabricated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Republic investigation found at least 27 of 41 articles contained fabricated material; examples include wholly made-up pieces like 'Hack Heaven' and fabricated quotations and incidents in others. Fabrication is grounds for firing, retraction, and reputational and legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of named and verifiable sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer named, identifiable sources over unnamed or partially identified sources; Glass's articles 'often relied on unnamed or partially identified sources.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymous sourcing made several of Glass's pieces difficult or impossible to verify; publications that could not verify anonymous-sourced material declined to vouch for it. Editors should demand verifiable attribution or additional corroboration when sources are anonymous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability of factual claims
rubrics_metrics.description: All factual claims should be corroboratable by independent records or evidence (e.g., company registrations, tax records, event venues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbes found no records for 'Jukt Micronics' and the California Franchise Tax Board reported no such company; hotel layout and opening dates undermined Glass's account of a conference. Basic checks (searches, government records, venue confirmations) can expose falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough fact-checking and editorial oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and fact-checkers must actively verify key elements of stories rather than rely solely on trust in a reporter; lapses in oversight enabled prolonged deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charles Lane only discovered errors after an external inquiry; The New Republic initially defended Glass. The article documents how 'normal human trust' without rigorous checks failed. Editors should have clear fact-checking procedures and follow up on unusual or sensational claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fabricate quotations or incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations and incidents quoted in reporting must be true and attributable; Glass fabricated quotations and incidents in multiple pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some Glass pieces contained 'real reporting interwoven with fabricated quotations and incidents.' Fabricating quotes is a severe ethical breach and frequently leads to retraction and loss of credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blending fact and fiction (clear factual boundary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a clear separation between fiction and journalism; do not interweave fabricated material with real reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fabulist (Glass's novel) is presented as fiction, but several magazine articles mixed fabricated elements with genuine reporting, which misled readers and fellow journalists. Any fictionalization must be clearly labeled as fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify primary-source artifacts and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm the authenticity of documents, websites, voice-mail accounts, business cards, and other artifacts provided by sources or reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glass 'created a website and voice mail account for Jukt Micronics, fabricating notes of story gathering, having fake business cards printed, and even composing editions of a fake newsletter' to thwart discovery. Editors should independently verify provenance of such materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution with anonymous-source-dependent verification
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting relies on anonymous sources, ensure additional corroboration because anonymity can limit external verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rolling Stone and Harper's found material generally accurate but 'maintained that they had no way of verifying the information because Glass had cited anonymous sources.' Use editorial policies to require corroboration for claims from anonymous sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retractions, corrections, and editorial accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications must correct the record and retract work when serious fabrications are discovered; editors should issue statements to readers and investigate past contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harper's retracted its story (its first in 165 years). The New Republic published statements and a report to readers after exposure. Retractions, transparent investigations, and public explanations are part of remedial editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restitution and remediation by the author
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects who have profited from fabricated reporting may make restitution as a form of remediation (monetary repayment, apologies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glass repaid Harper's $10,000 and stated he repaid $200,000 to multiple publications. While repayment does not undo harm, it is recorded as part of attempts to 'make right' transgressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure and honesty in later proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronted, the individual must fully disclose the extent of wrongdoing; incomplete admissions damage credibility further (especially in legal or licensing contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The California Supreme Court criticized Glass for not admitting the full extent of his fabrications until the 2007 moral character proceedings; 'hypocrisy and evasiveness' in testimony undermined his claim of reform and contributed to denial of admission to the bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional moral character affects licensing and careers
rubrics_metrics.description: Severe ethical breaches in journalism can be considered by licensing and professional bodies when evaluating moral fitness for other professions (e.g., law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glass passed bar exams but was refused certification on moral-fitness grounds; the Committee of Bar Examiners cited ethics concerns stemming from his journalistic malpractice, and the California Supreme Court ultimately denied admission due to persistent dishonesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative indicators for detecting fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for concrete inconsistencies (nonexistent organizations, mismatched venue descriptions, false legislative claims) as red flags for fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples that exposed Glass included nonexistent company 'Jukt Micronics', hotel layouts that did not match the article's description, false claims about state legislation or conferences, and phone numbers that traced back to the reporter or his associates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial response: re-examination of past contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: After exposure of fabrication, publications should re-examine other contributions from the implicated reporter and transparently report findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New Republic, Rolling Stone, George, and Harper's re-examined Glass's contributions after his exposure; some publications found additional fabrications and noted inability to verify other pieces. Systematic review helps restore editorial integrity.
